## Findings by module

### 3

- **extended** (ch-008.txt): Block's depth cues, ranked by his order: convergence (camera angle makes parallel lines meet at vanishing points), size change (staging in depth), textural diffusion, object and camera movement (relative movement, with dolly, track or crane), aerial diffusion (fog, smoke, snow), tonal and colour separation, up/down position against the horizon, shape change, overlap, focus. Dolly example: a 3-foot push takes an actor at 5 feet to 2 feet but one at 100 feet only 3% closer. Use as the course's depth-cue checklist; the ranking is his.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt): Block's flat, limited and ambiguous space, with the key lens claim: a zoom keeps space flat because all planes change size together (no relative movement), a dolly keeps depth; a telephoto lens does not flatten space optically, the flattening comes from the staging and cues. Also: a tracking or crane move parallel to a flat wall keeps flat space. Good for the course's lens and move sections; it corrects a common belief.
- **extended** (ch-008.txt): Block on open space: it is hard to make because the frame lines keep a picture closed. Open space comes from a very large screen, strong random or in-out movement that overwhelms the frame, removing stationary lines (a horizon kills it), or removing the frame (VR). Also the Principle of Contrast and Affinity applied to space: deep is more intense because most depth cues are contrasts.
- **note** (ch-006.txt): Block's seven visual components (space, line, shape, tone, colour, movement, rhythm) and his three ways a picture communicates (story, sound, visuals). His 'visual progression' point, line, plane, volume is a checklist for building a shot's intensity. Useful as the course's composition vocabulary; he notes that 'red means danger' is only a stereotype, not a rule.
- **note** (ch-008.txt): Block's surface divisions (halves, thirds, grids, square on rectangle, golden section) and his aspect-ratio facts: 1.85:1 standard theatrical, 2.39:1 scope, 1.78:1 (16x9) digital TV. Use as the course's frame-shape and split-frame checklist; examples are his film stills.
- **note** (ch-016.txt): Block's directorial beats (appendix C): a scene split into beats where the relationship changes; each beat can be shown by acting, staging, camera, editing or a change in the visual components. His example moves the linear motif from contrast to affinity as the characters agree. Good for the course's coverage planning.

### 4

- **extended** (ch-009.txt): Block's line rules, a practical checklist for the lighting and set-dressing sections: a line is seen only where there is tonal contrast; a shape or line can be found by squinting or with a contrast-viewing glass, which reveals the linear motif; then light and dress to keep the motif the story needs. Seven ways lines appear: edge, contour, closure, plane intersection, axis, distance, track. Verticals, horizontals and diagonals carry different intensity.
- **extended** (ch-010.txt): Block on controlling tone three ways: art direction (reflective: the actual paint and costume), lighting (incident: light and shadow), and exposure (lens, whole frame only). Coincidence of tone: the tonal range reveals the subject; non-coincidence hides it (a face in shadow in All the President's Men, Kurtz in Apocalypse Now). Hiding the subject shifts attention to sound. Test with a black-and-white monitor or contrast glass to keep colour from hiding tone. Core for the course's lighting module.

### 6

- **refined** (ch-011.txt): Block calls magic hour shadowless blue daylight. Magic hour is warm and soft (golden hour); the blue is the period after sunset (blue hour). Check the two before using either term in the course.
- **contradicted** (ch-011.txt): Block says a prism shows sunlight is predominantly blue. Direct sunlight has a fairly even spectrum that reads as near-white, peaking in green-yellow, and its colour temperature is about 5500 to 5800 K; the blue look is skylight and shade. Correct before the course repeats it.
- **extended** (ch-011.txt): Block's colour practice, usable for the course's colour and grading sections: Albers' simultaneous contrast rules (lightness, saturation, hue shift), warm/cool contrast, and colour scripts in place of words; the colour palette as the strongest control (paint and costume first, then lights and filters, then grading); filters subtract, so a yellow filter removes blue. Pair with the cinematography book's colour-balance notes.

### 5

- **extended** (ch-012.txt): Block's movement vocabulary for the course's camera-move section: actual, induced, apparent and relative movement. Only relative movement matters on screen, so a camera that keeps pace with its subject shows no movement. Three-dimensional moves (dolly, track, crane) create relative movement; pan, tilt and zoom do not. A snap zoom adds intensity. Level versus non-level framing turns verticals and horizontals into diagonals. He also gives a continuum grid to plan where the audience looks shot to shot (affinity cuts stay invisible).
- **extended** (ch-013.txt): Block on continuous versus fragmented events, for the course's coverage decision: break an event into sub-events, then choose one continuous take (the camera must be right throughout; no later editing control) or coverage (contrast and affinity and rhythm can be set shot by shot). Shot-level rhythm is alternation, repetition and tempo; editorial rhythm is strongest where shot-to-shot contrast is strongest. A moving object alone is not rhythm.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Block's three choices for any visual component across a production: constant (one look throughout, for unity), progression (gradual change, motivated by the story), or contrast and affinity (spikes at story peaks). Example: a trapped family in flat or deep space that is established in the exposition. Ninotchka's one deep-space entrance is the cue he gives for contrast. Use this as the course's rule for choosing one constant look and a few deliberate changes.
- **note** (ch-012.txt): Block's shot-to-shot continuum: affinity (the eye stays in one quadrant across the cut) makes cuts invisible and can hide screen-direction errors; contrast (the eye must jump) makes a cut jarring. Plan the sequence on a storyboard that shows the eye's path. Split screens work only when one panel holds critical information.
- **note** (ch-013.txt): Block's three rhythm sources (stationary lines, moving objects that enter, exit or change direction, and editing) and his flow-line idea: plot the story's rhythm as peaks and valleys. Use as the course's pacing note; the examples are his.
- **note** (ch-014.txt): Block's two-graph method: plot the story's conflict intensity on one graph, then plot a visual component (for example space, flat or deep) on a second graph below it, and ask whether each component is a constant, a progression, or a deliberate change. Use as the course's planning method for shot-by-shot design. Examples are his (Jaws, Get Out, North by Northwest).
- **note** (ch-015.txt): Block's practice points for the course's planning section: decide a point of view first (how the film should make the audience feel), then choose components by analytic, researched, instinctive or arbitrary choice; ask 'what should I remove from the shot' (visual economy); and keep the rules few and consistent, because visual rules are a framework, not law. Good closing advice for the course.
